findings.location: §8, 'Paired-difference standard error', lines 370–378
findings.description: The worked example equates one standard error with a resolvable effect: 'Paired, same 100 items, discordance pd=0.25 → SE ≈ √(0.25/100) = 0.050 — a same-item design resolves a ~5-point difference where the (wrong, for correlated data) two-sample calculation would demand ~6.7 points.' The verb 'resolves' is defined two paragraphs earlier as MDE ('this design resolves a ~17-point paired difference and no smaller one'). By the chapter's own formula, the same design's MDE is (1.96+0.84)×√(0.25/100) = 0.140, i.e. 14 points paired and 18.8 points two-sample — 2.8× the numbers printed. A reader applying this example to the accompanying p₁=0.70 vs p₂=0.60 comparison concludes a 10-point gap is resolvable at n=100 when the design's own MDE floor makes it INCONCLUSIVE. This is the sub-MDE-to-difference promotion that P9, §9's REJECTED list, and global tripwire #6 all exist to forbid, demonstrated in the canonical example of the governing chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Report MDEs, not SEs, whenever the sentence claims resolution: 'paired SE 0.050 vs two-sample 0.067 → MDE 14pp vs 18.8pp at α=.05/power=.80 — a 25% tighter interval for free, but neither design resolves the 10-point gap in this example, which is INCONCLUSIVE.' Reserve 'resolves' for MDE everywhere in the chapter.

findings.location: §3a, 'Vendor power table', lines 119–127
findings.description: The table is indexed by discordant-pair count alone (10/50/100/500/1000 → 28%/12.5%/8.8%/3.9%/2.8%) with the MDE column's units unstated, and it cannot be reproduced from the formula stated ten lines above it. In rate-difference units (δ = (n₁₀−n₀₁)/N, the units §3a itself defines), MDE = (z_α/2+z_β)·pd/√n_d — it depends on pd/N, not on n_d alone. Every row of the table implies pd = 0.316 (I checked all five: MDE·√n_d = 0.885, 0.884, 0.880, 0.872, 0.885), i.e. the table silently assumes N ≈ 3.16·n_d. In discordant-split units (q vs 0.5, which is what the header's 'exact binomial test' actually tests), the correct values are 88.6%/39.6%/28%/12.5%/8.9% — the table's row values are the correct values for a 10× larger n_d, i.e. shifted one column. Consequence: used for the pre-data sizing the text recommends, the table understates MDE for high-discordance designs — at n_d=100 with pd=0.427 (the realized discordance in this playbook's own CASE-002) the true MDE is 12.0pp, not the tabulated 8.8pp — so a contract sized off it pre-registers an MDE the design cannot deliver, and an observed 10pp gap then reads as 'above MDE'.
findings.suggested_fix: Either state the units and the assumption ('MDE on the overall pass-rate difference, at the vendor's assumed discordance pd≈0.32 / equivalently N≈3.16·n_d — do not use at other discordances'), or replace the table with the chapter's own MDE ≈ (z_α/2+z_power)·√(pd/N_eff) evaluated on a pd × N grid, and keep the vendor row only as a cross-check at its own pd.

findings.location: §8 'Verdict vocabulary' lines 450–454 and §7 stop-condition table line 311; GLOSSARY.md 'descriptive vocabulary' lines 180–184; against 00_PRINCIPLES_AND_SCOPE.md P9 lines 115–121 and tripwire #6 lines 230–231
findings.description: Chapter 00 P9 states without exception that sub-MDE results are 'INCONCLUSIVE, never "equivalent" or "no difference"', and tripwire #6 fires when a sub-MDE result 'is being read as a difference or an equivalence'. Chapter 04 and the glossary then create an exception: a pre-registered 'descriptive vocabulary' ('materially better', 'competitive', 'materially worse') licenses a descriptive reading of a sub-MDE result. Pre-registration fixes who chose the words and when; it cannot supply resolving power the data lack. 'Competitive (within ±d)' is an equivalence claim and 'materially better/worse' is a comparative inferential claim, and neither requires an equivalence test (TOST), a margin d ≥ MDE, or any power statement. The playbook's own flagship demonstration shows the harm: examples/SYNTH-09 prints 'Candidate-Upgrade is "competitive (within ±9pp)"' as the licensed reading of a result whose cluster-robust 95% CI is [−3pp, +11pp] — an interval that leaves the ±9pp band, so even a proper equivalence test at margin 9pp would fail. The rule as written lets a team retire a candidate comparison with an equivalence-shaped sentence the data contradict.
findings.suggested_fix: Constrain the license: descriptive categories MAY NOT assert equivalence or direction; a 'competitive'/'no material difference' category requires a pre-registered equivalence margin plus a TOST (or a CI contained in ±d) and is otherwise INCONCLUSIVE. Fix SYNTH-09 to report 'INCONCLUSIVE; CI [−3, +11] pp does not exclude an 11-point gain', and make chapter 00 P9 and tripwire #6 state the exception explicitly rather than reading as absolute.

findings.location: §9 'Routing break-even', false-negative extension, lines 432–449
findings.description: The extension s* = (C_gate + e·L)/(C_strong − C_weak) charges the expected misroute cost e·L to every item, including the (1−s) fraction the gate escalated — items that by construction cannot produce a gate false negative. A false negative is an item kept at the weak tier that should have escalated, so its cost accrues only on the offloaded share: avg_cost(s) = C_gate + s·C_weak + (1−s)·C_strong + s·e·L, and break-even against always-strong is s* = C_gate/(C_strong − C_weak − e·L). On the file's own numbers (C_gate=$0.01, C_weak=$0.02, C_strong=$0.30, e=0.05, L=$2.00) the correct bar is 5.6%, not the stated 39.3%; the headline 'raised the bar roughly elevenfold' is an artifact of the misallocation (the true factor is ~1.6×). The error's direction kills routing projects that actually pay: a team measuring a 20% offload share would reject routing on a bar of 39.3% that should read 5.6%. The two forms coincide only at the infeasibility boundary the text mentions (e·L ≥ C_strong − C_weak), which is why the surrounding prose reads as consistent.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with s* = C_gate/(C_strong − C_weak − e·L), rework the worked example (0.01/(0.28−0.10) ≈ 5.6%) and the 'elevenfold' sentence, and state that e is the false-negative rate among offloaded items (and that e and s move together as the gate threshold moves, so s* is a bound, not a sweep).

findings.location: §8 'Verdict vocabulary' table, lines 443–448 (with §5 Step 12, lines 222–226)
findings.description: INCONCLUSIVE is defined as 'the observed effect (or its absence) is smaller than the design's MDE' — a comparison of an observed effect against a pre-data power quantity, i.e. post-hoc power reasoning. The glossary (which claims precedence over chapters) defines it correctly as a property of the design: 'the design could not resolve the question at its MDE'. Two concrete failures follow. (a) Uncovered cell in a closed vocabulary: observed effect above MDE but the primary statistic does not cross the threshold (e.g. δ=0.20, MDE=0.17, p=0.09) is not CONFIRMED, not REFUTED, not INCONCLUSIVE as defined, not RANKED — yet §12 requires the report to print 'one of CONFIRMED / REFUTED / INCONCLUSIVE / RANKED'. The path of least resistance is to call it CONFIRMED because it 'clears MDE'. (b) The converse: a nominally significant result below MDE is forced to INCONCLUSIVE, discarding a valid pre-registered inference. Both come from using the point estimate rather than the interval as the discriminator.
findings.suggested_fix: Key the verdicts to the pre-registered test and its interval: CONFIRMED when the primary statistic crosses the threshold in the predicted direction; REFUTED when it crosses against prediction or a gate fails; INCONCLUSIVE otherwise — including every non-crossing result — with the MDE reported alongside as the statement of what the design could have resolved. Align the glossary and Step 12 with the same wording.

findings.location: §4 'Screening ranks; only a frozen comparison infers' (lines 89–94) and 'No candidate is eliminated on a margin the design cannot resolve' (lines 96–103), with §5 Step 5 (lines 181–186)
findings.description: The elimination rule is stated absolutely — 'no candidate is withdrawn from selection on a margin smaller than the pilot's own MDE' — while Step 5 mandates ASHA-style successive-halving rungs for screening more than two candidates. Successive halving drops the bottom 1−1/η of candidates by rank at every rung, on margins that are arbitrarily small and typically far below any rung's MDE; that is the mechanism, not an implementation detail. The chapter never says which rule governs, so the two normative statements are in direct conflict and a candidate can be eliminated at rung 1 on noise and never reach the frozen comparison — the elimination-rule failure mode, relocated upstream where the chapter's own guards don't look. Note the cited source (EXT-STOPPING-003) also covers Hoeffding/Bernstein racing, which eliminates only when a confidence bound separates candidates and therefore does satisfy the elimination rule; the chapter lumps the two families together.
findings.suggested_fix: State the precedence explicitly: rank-based rungs may only defer/suspend candidates (revivable at the frozen comparison), while permanent elimination requires either a racing confidence bound (Hoeffding/Bernstein at the cluster level) or a margin ≥ the rung's MDE. If rank-based elimination is accepted as a deliberate cost, say so in the elimination-rule principle and record the risk, rather than leaving two absolutes to collide.

findings.location: §8 'Curtailment arithmetic' lines 389–402 and §6 [PARAMETER] 'Curtailment bar and tolerance k' lines 245–250; formulary §6a lines 234–261
findings.description: Certainty curtailment's correctness proof is sound but narrow: it shows the arm's *observed* count cannot reach ⌈bar×N⌉, hence halting reproduces the decision completion would have made. It says nothing about whether the arm's *true* rate is below the bar, and its consequence is defined as 'irreversible rejection'. Nothing in the chapter requires N to be sized so the bar decision is resolvable, so an arm whose certain interval is, say, [0.58, 0.599] against bar 0.60 is permanently eliminated on a shortfall far inside the design's MDE — exactly what §4's elimination rule forbids for selection margins, with no stated reason why absolute gates are exempt. The verdict table quietly grants the exemption ('REFUTED … or a pre-registered gate fails outright') without acknowledging it, so the MDE/INCONCLUSIVE discipline has a licensed bypass whenever a decision is phrased as a bar rather than a margin.
findings.suggested_fix: State the gate/MDE precedence in one sentence — either 'absolute gates are decision rules, not inferences, and are deliberately exempt from the MDE floor; size N so that bar ± MDE is not straddled' or 'curtailment's rejection is irreversible only when the certain interval's upper bound falls below bar by at least the design's MDE; otherwise it halts to a RE-RUN/defer state'. Add a freeze-gate row requiring the bar's own resolvability to be computed.

findings.description: Chapter 04 declares i.i.d.-calibrated sequential rules 'admissible only after a passed independence check', and §9's REJECTED is conditioned on the check being absent — so 'passed' is the load-bearing term in the entire rejection. findings.location: P4 lines 75–81 and §9 'Speed rationales for stopping rules' lines 247–249; echoed in 04 §8 lines 404–409, 04 §9 lines 461–464, formulary §6 line 303
findings.description: P4 is labeled (strong-evidence) and asserts two universals — 'The scarce resources of a small lab are operator attention and measurement validity, not compute' and stopping rules' 'measured wall-clock value is typically small' — citing only [CASE: CASE-001]. Chapter 04 §8 restates it as a general empirical fact ('the arms that consume the most wall clock in practice are the ones near the decision boundary, which rarely trigger it'), and §9/00 §9 render it as an unconditional [REJECTED] ('condition: always — these are generically wrong'). The underlying measurement, read in CASE-001, is one milestone on one project: curtailment would have saved 0.51h of 24h (~2%) *because that project's dominant arm sat near its qualification bar*. That is a project parameter, not a universal — on a suite where hopeless arms dominate wall clock, or where per-item cost is large, curtailment's speed value is genuinely large and a speed rationale is not wrong per se. P12 explicitly forbids rendering a single project's result as consensus, and P10 shows the authors know how to label this honestly ('case-study + inference').
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel P4 as (case-study + inference) or split it (the attention/validity claim as inference; the wall-clock claim as case-study, scoped to CASE-001's conditions), and condition the rejection: '[REJECTED] (condition: the rationale trades away curtailment's guards, or the arms dominating wall clock sit near the decision boundary — measure before claiming savings)'. Keep the real invariant, which is that the guards are non-negotiable regardless of motive.
