findings.location: §8, 'pass^k (reliability under repetition)', lines 386–389; echoed in 04 §8 line 432
findings.description: 'pass^k = p^k' is stated without noting that p is *per task*. Averaging over heterogeneous tasks, the fraction of tasks that succeed k/k is E[p_i^k] ≥ (E[p_i])^k by Jensen, so substituting an aggregate pass rate — the obvious move given that the section's only worked inputs are scalar p values — understates true pass^k, and the gap grows with k and with difficulty spread. The section warns about the opposite failure (correlated failures collapsing pass^k faster) but not this one, and the 'when this breaks' list does not mention it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one line: 'p is per-task; pass^k is measured as the share of tasks succeeding on all k independent attempts, not as (aggregate pass rate)^k — the latter understates it whenever task difficulty varies.'

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — statistical core (00_PRINCIPLES_AND_SCOPE, 04_EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_AND_STATISTICS, references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS, GLOSSARY), with source rows checked against references/sources.yaml and worked numbers recomputed independently
findings.location: §12 'Prediction-ledger scoring', worked example, lines 574–582
findings.description: The example applies the worst-case (p=0.5) margin 0.98/√20 = 21.9 points to an observed p̂ = 0.70 at n = 20, which violates two conditions the file states elsewhere: §11's 'when this breaks' says the worst-case form is 'for pre-data sizing only' once p̂ is known, and §1 says to use an exact (Clopper–Pearson) interval once n·(1−p̂) < ~10 — here it is 6. The Wald interval at p̂=0.70 is [49.9%, 90.1%] and an exact interval is wider and asymmetric; the conclusion (70% is not yet distinguishable from a calibrated 80%) survives either way, so this is a self-consistency defect rather than a wrong answer.
findings.suggested_fix: Compute the example with an exact interval (or at least with p̂(1−p̂)) and note explicitly why the worst-case shortcut was not used, so the file's flagship calibration example does not model the shortcut it forbids.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — statistical core (00_PRINCIPLES_AND_SCOPE, 04_EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_AND_STATISTICS, references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS, GLOSSARY), with source rows checked against references/sources.yaml and worked numbers recomputed independently
findings.location: §8 curtailment guards, lines 393–402 (with §4 lines 66–75)
findings.description: Certainty curtailment requires computing the running pass count on a qualify/confirm arm mid-run — a genuine interim read of held-out outcomes. Its admissibility argument rests entirely on 'its only possible consequence is irreversibly rejecting an already-spent arm', but nothing in the chapter or the contract template requires the interim statistic to be blinded to the operator or restricted to the runner. The amendment-legitimacy gate blocks the worst path (condition 3 bars amendments after qualify/confirm execution begins), and guard 2 blocks partial point reporting, but nothing prevents the interim rate informing other in-flight choices (which arms to keep running, what to expect, how to frame the write-up) — which is precisely the mid-run investigator judgment §4's first principle removes.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a fourth guard or a sentence to guard 1: 'the curtailment statistic is computed by the runner and exposed only as HALT/CONTINUE; interim pass counts on a qualify/confirm arm are not disclosed to the operator before the arm completes or halts.'

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — statistical core (00_PRINCIPLES_AND_SCOPE, 04_EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_AND_STATISTICS, references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS, GLOSSARY), with source rows checked against references/sources.yaml and worked numbers recomputed independently
findings.location: §7 [DECISION GATE] 'Freeze gate' table, lines 265–278
findings.description: The freeze gate is written as an unconditional obligation ('Before the first iterate-split item executes, all of the following MUST be true') and requires a content-hash-bound contract, a prediction-ledger entry, and look-ledger rows. Chapter 00 §6 assigns exactly these artifacts to Tier 2 and above (Tier 1 gets 'lightweight profile; notes-grade pinned provenance'). Chapter 04 §2 hedges that the stakes tier 'fixes how much of this chapter's machinery is mandatory', but the gate table itself carries no tier qualifier, so a Tier-1 exploratory pilot reading §7 is told the full contract is mandatory — inviting either over-compliance or, worse, selective disregard of a table whose other rows are load-bearing at every tier.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a tier column or a header clause to the gate table ('rows 1, 3, 7, 8 apply at Tier 2+; the never-skippable floor items apply at every tier'), matching chapter 00 §6's mapping.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §6 Parameters, lines 432–435
findings.description: The normative parameter is inverted. Text: "**[PARAMETER] Passing/recall threshold per stratum.** Set above the stratum's measured ceiling with margin, never equal to it (§8.1)". The parameter being defined is the threshold, so this instructs the reader to set the passing threshold ABOVE the measured reachability ceiling. That is the exact condition chapter 00's global tripwire #2 and this chapter's own STOP CONDITION (line 465) define as a broken instrument: "A stratum's measured ceiling is below its passing threshold ... Fix the instrument before reading any score." It also contradicts the section it cites: §8.1 says "set the threshold comfortably below the ceiling (e.g., ceiling ≥ threshold + 0.05)" and §8.4 says "The stratum's reachability ceiling MUST exceed this bar with margin." A reader following §6 makes every stratum unwinnable by construction.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite as: "Set below the stratum's measured ceiling with margin, never equal to it (§8.1) — the ceiling must exceed the threshold by at least the declared margin (illustrative: ceiling ≥ threshold + 0.05)." Add a static integrity gate that fails a release when any stratum's threshold ≥ its measured ceiling, so the inversion cannot survive in a project's config even if the prose is misread.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.1 rung table (column 4, lines 125–136); §7 "[DECISION GATE] Rung descent" (lines 319–321); consumed by 09 §2 line 37–39 and 09 §4 condition (2)
findings.description: The column "Evidence required to move past it" carries two incompatible semantics. Rungs 0–4 hold exit criteria ("Static integrity gates green", "Tool contract audit passed", "variants show no further pre-registered gain"). Rungs 5–9 hold entry criteria — the conditions for *doing* the rung, not for having exhausted it: rung 5 is "Truncation-rate tolerance breached ... and a diagnostic shows the residual truncation is where the gap actually lives"; rung 6 is "Oracle analysis shows a meaningful ceiling gain; a routing break-even is achievable; a deterministic gate is insufficient"; rung 7 is the train-at-all gate itself (identically restated in 09 §4). §7 then binds on this column: "Moving to a cheaper-diagnosed-but-costlier rung requires the 'evidence required to move past it' column of §5.1 to be satisfied for every rung above the target." Applied literally, reaching rung 7 requires satisfying rung 6's row — i.e. requires that oracle analysis shows a meaningful routing gain and a routing break-even is achievable — which is a condition for building a router, and which is *false* precisely when routing is inapplicable and descent is legitimate. Consequence: 09 §2's precondition "Chapter 07's evidence that rungs 0–6 are exhausted" and 09 §4 condition (2) "cheaper rungs are exhausted with evidence" have no operational definition for rungs 5 and 6 — the two rungs immediately above fine-tuning. Chapter 14 §2 uses the opposite (entry) semantics throughout ("Descend only with: rungs 0–2 cleared"), confirming the two readings are live in the same playbook. In practice a reader asserts budget and routing exhaustion against nothing checkable, and the evidence bar stops binding exactly where premature training happens.
findings.suggested_fix: Split the column into two: "Entry evidence (this rung is indicated)" and "Exit evidence (this rung is exhausted)", and fill the exit column for rungs 5–9 explicitly — e.g. rung 5 exit: "cap re-derived from the current artifact's own iterate-split distribution, truncation rate inside its tolerance at the pre-registered headroom quantile, and a §5.2 diagnostic showing residual truncation is not where the gap lives"; rung 6 exit: "oracle analysis shows the between-tier ceiling gain is below the routing break-even, OR a gate was built and the residual gap persists under a paired comparison". Then restate §7's rung-descent gate to bind on the exit column only, and have 09 §2 cite that column by name.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §7 "[DECISION GATE] Judge-trust gate" (lines 460–463), against §5.7 (lines 271–302)
findings.description: The gate has no pass criterion. Its rule is procedural completeness: "no judge score drives a decision until all seven steps of §5.7 are complete and reported", with outcomes "trusted-for-decision / directional-only / not usable yet" — but nothing maps a κ value, a CI width, or a bias-audit result onto those three outcomes, and nothing anywhere requires a minimum κ to be pre-registered before the calibration data is seen. A team can complete all seven steps, report κ = 0.25 with a CI spanning 0.05–0.45, and the gate is satisfied on its own terms. This is the single defense standing between an uncalibrated judge and a decision, and it cannot fail. It is also a direct inconsistency with P7 ("Decision-driving thresholds are fixed before data") and with this chapter's own §6 parameter, which presupposes a bar exists ("size the human-anchor set to resolve the κ confidence interval the decision needs") without ever requiring one to be declared. Contrast 07 §5.2 step 3, which does this correctly: pre-registered GO/RE-SCOPE/DROP bands plus a sufficiency floor, fixed before running.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an eighth step to §5.7: "Pre-register the minimum κ (and the maximum acceptable CI width) that licenses each of the three gate outcomes, before the anchor set is scored, as a consequence-bearing tolerance." Restate the §7 gate rule as: all seven steps complete AND κ's lower confidence bound ≥ the pre-registered bar → trusted-for-decision; κ point estimate ≥ bar but lower bound below it → directional-only; otherwise not usable yet. Make the bar a [PARAMETER] in §6 with tier-scaled guidance rather than a universal number.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.5 quantization acceptance gates (lines 249–271), §8 quantization worked example (lines 379–386), §7 stop condition (lines 354–356)
findings.description: The quantization acceptance gate is the one decision-driving comparison in the playbook that escapes the statistics canon entirely. `recovery% = task_score(quantized) / task_score(higher-precision baseline) × 100` is a ratio of two point estimates; §5.5, §6's parameter row, §7's stop condition and §8's worked example contain no N, no confidence interval, no MDE, no paired design, and no INCONCLUSIVE outcome. §8's example ships the anti-pattern verbatim: "Baseline task score 82.0; PTQ-only quantized score 79.5 → recovery ≈ 97.0% ... proceed to the next escalation step" — a 2.5-point difference read as a decision with no statement of how many items produced it or whether the design can resolve 2.5 points. Chapter 00 §9 lists "Promoting sub-MDE margins to decisions" as generically wrong, P9 requires a pre-computed MDE on every comparison, and 09 §8 says explicitly "Nothing in fine-tuning licenses a different statistical standard for 'did this help'" — yet quantization, a ship/no-ship decision, gets exactly that. A project following §5.5 can ship a degraded artifact, or reject a good one, on noise.
findings.suggested_fix: Bind §5.5 to chapter 04: require the quantized-vs-baseline comparison to be paired on the same items, with N_eff, MDE and a CI on the recovery ratio (or on the paired score difference) stated before the run; require the verdict vocabulary CONFIRMED / REFUTED / INCONCLUSIVE; and state that a recovery estimate whose CI spans the pre-registered bar is INCONCLUSIVE, not a pass. Rework the §8 worked example to carry N, the interval, and an explicit MDE check. Note also that the vendor's >99% figure is a *median across a benchmark suite* of per-benchmark recoveries, so importing it as a bar on a single aggregate score changes the statistic — say so at the point of use.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.2 canonical failure taxonomy, RC-1 (line 176) and RC-7 (line 182)
findings.description: The taxonomy asserts exactly-one membership ("every project-specific root cause ... classifies into exactly one of these twelve generic classes") but RC-1 and RC-7 share their defining noun with no discriminator, and they route to opposite ends of the ladder. RC-1: "The eval, ground truth, or grader is wrong (unreachable required evidence, wrong gold, grader polarity, ceiling below threshold)" → Rung 0, "no other result is interpretable". RC-7: "Verification gap — The verifier/grader passes failures silently" → Rung 4. A team whose scorer marks wrong answers as passes matches RC-7's text more literally than RC-1's, and RC-7 sends them to prompt/workflow/verifier work while they continue trusting every score the suite produces. That is precisely the failure P2 and rung 0 exist to prevent, reached by following the taxonomy as written. Nothing in 03, 07 §5.1, 14 §2, or the GLOSSARY entry states the intended distinction (eval-side instrument vs. the system-under-test's own verifier), and the GLOSSARY's "silent failure" entry anchors RC-7 to the taxonomy without disambiguating either.
findings.suggested_fix: Rename and re-scope: RC-1 → "Evaluation-instrument defect (the eval harness, corpus, gold answers, or *evaluation* grader is wrong)"; RC-7 → "In-system verification gap (the *system's own* verifier or guard passes failures silently at inference time)". Add one disambiguating line under the table: "If the defective component is part of the execution system under test, it is RC-7 (rung 4). If it is part of the measuring instrument, it is RC-1 (rung 0). When in doubt, treat it as RC-1 — the cost of an unnecessary instrument check is bounded; the cost of trusting a broken instrument is not." Propagate to GLOSSARY and 14.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.description: Two evidence labels are inflated past what the chapter's own bodies and the cited ledger rows support, and the chapter applies an inconsistent standard within one section. (a) "A costly experiment earns its cost only after a cheap diagnostic clears it. (strong-evidence)" — the body then says "First-principles argument: ...", and the corroboration offered is one vendor blog (NV-AGENTICBLOGS-001, evidence_strength: consensus, a framing statement not a study) plus a single internal case (CASE-011, n=1). Under the playbook's own evidence-strength vocabulary this is `inference` or `case-study + inference`. Chapter 00's P10 labels a structurally identical claim honestly as "(case-study + inference)", and two paragraphs later this same section labels "Completion is not correctness" correctly as "(inference — first-principles, corroborated by case evidence)". (b) "Descend the ladder on evidence, not on the calendar. (strong-evidence)" attaches strong-evidence to a ten-rung total order, while the cited EXT-FT-001 ("three studies agree RAG/prompt-first for factual/citation tasks") supports only one edge of that order in one task family, and the chapter itself states two paragraphs down that rungs 1–6 MAY be re-sequenced — i.e. most of the order is neither normative nor evidenced. This is P12's failure mode ("a single project's result is never rendered as consensus") committed by the playbook.
findings.suggested_fix: Relabel (a) as "(inference — first-principles; case-study corroboration, n=1)". For (b), keep strong-evidence only on the evidenced content and state its scope inline: "strong-evidence for {rung 0 first; rungs 2–4 before rung 7 on knowledge/citation tasks}; inference for the relative ordering of rungs 3–6 and 8–9, which is a cost ordering, not an empirical finding."

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §4 lines 61–67; §5.6 line 261; §9 lines 560–562; propagated to 00 P11 (line 134–139) and 00 §9
findings.description: The playbook's most-repeated empirical claim overstates its source's scope and omits the baseline that makes the number meaningful. Text: "An LLM judge scoring an objectively checkable output — execution result, schema conformance, exact/fuzzy match — performs near chance: one controlled study measured a frontier judge at roughly 56.6% on verifiable tasks [EXT-JUDGE-002]." The sources.yaml row (line 865–879) identifies EXT-JUDGE-002 as JudgeBench (arXiv:2410.12784), whose task is pairwise discrimination between a correct and an incorrect response on challenging knowledge/reasoning/math/coding items. 56.6% is "near chance" only because that is a two-alternative forced choice with a 50% floor — a fact the chapter never states, leaving a reader with an open-ended rubric unable to map the number onto anything. Worse, the three examples the chapter attaches to the finding ("execution result, schema conformance, exact/fuzzy match") are exactly the grading modes JudgeBench does not measure, and where a judge would not plausibly be near chance. The prescription (prefer the deterministic check where one exists) is right on other grounds — determinism, cost, auditability — but the evidence as presented is stretched, and it is stretched identically in four places.
findings.suggested_fix: State the study's design at first use: "JudgeBench measures pairwise discrimination between a correct and an incorrect response on hard knowledge/reasoning/math/coding items; a frontier judge scored ~56.6% against a 50% chance floor." Then narrow the generalization to what follows — that judges are unreliable at discriminating correctness on hard items — and justify the deterministic default on determinism/cost/auditability grounds for the trivially-checkable cases (schema, exact match) rather than borrowing JudgeBench's number for them.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §4 lines 69–76; §6 "Position B — curation" lines 410–412
findings.description: The chapter's headline instrument-defect evidence is a cross-version pass-rate difference used in exactly the way the chapter forbids elsewhere, with an unsupported causal attribution on top. Text: "Human-reviewing a widely used benchmark down from 1,699 to 500 tasks moved its measured solve rate on the *same models* from 16% to 33.2% [EXT-EVAL-005]: most of that swing was instrument noise, not capability." The 16% and 33.2% figures are measured on two different item sets — the 500 kept items are a non-random, human-selected subset of the 1,699 — so the delta confounds instrument-defect removal with a shift in sample difficulty. No published decomposition of the 17.2 points into those components exists, and sources.yaml (lines 805–819) claims only the raw figures, not the attribution. "Most of that swing was instrument noise" is therefore the playbook's inference asserted as fact under a strong-evidence label. This collides with two of the chapter's own rules: §5.9's "A raw score delta across two instrument versions is not a capability measurement. Decompose it", and §9's REJECTED "Cross-version score subtraction". It is also the mirror image of the selection-effect caveat 07 §5.3 step 6 requires "wherever a rescue/conversion rate is reported".
findings.suggested_fix: Report the figures without the attribution: "...moved the measured solve rate from 16% on the full set to 33.2% on the curated subset — a delta that mixes removal of invalid items with a change in the item population, and that no published analysis decomposes." Then make the pedagogical point the chapter actually needs — that a large share of a measured score can be a property of the corpus rather than the model — and cite CASE-004, which does supply a decomposed, same-corpus demonstration (7 spurious forbidden-claim flags; 91.7% → 99.0%).

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.7 steps 3 and 4, lines 286–288
findings.description: Two of the seven mandatory calibration steps are phenomenon names with no procedure, no threshold, and no consequence, so they cannot fail: "3. **Bias audits.** Position bias, length bias, self-preference, style bias." and "4. **Rubric stability across paraphrase.** The same answer, reworded, should not change the verdict." Nothing states how many paraphrases, what flip rate is disqualifying, what the audit's output artifact is, or what happens on a breach — in a playbook whose central doctrine is that "a detection without a consequence is not a control" (00 P7). Separately, the named bias set is the pairwise-preference literature's list: position bias is only defined when the judge sees two responses in an order, but §5.6 licenses judges for scoring open-ended output, which is often single-output. The protocol therefore mandates an audit that may not apply to the reader's judging mode while omitting the control that always applies — the protocol never requires the judge to be blind to which arm produced the output, despite the chapter being fastidious about blinding in its gold-label boundary (§4, §5.4).
findings.suggested_fix: Specify each audit as a measurable quantity with a pre-registered tolerance and consequence: position bias as verdict-flip rate under order swap on a paired subsample (pairwise judges only); length/verbosity bias as the judge's score-vs-output-length slope on items with equal ground-truth quality; self-preference as score delta on outputs from the judge's own family; paraphrase stability as verdict-flip rate over k pre-registered paraphrases. Add an explicit arm-blinding requirement: the judge's input must not identify the arm, and any identifying artifact (formatting, IDs, model self-reference) is a structural-leakage finding under §5.8.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.7 step 1 (line 279–281) and step 2, against §6 non-generator instruments (lines 394–397)
findings.description: The protocol never requires the human-anchor set's own reliability to be measured, so a reported κ is uninterpretable. Step 1 says only "Stratified sample against a human-anchor set — labels the judge is compared to, not trained on." κ(judge, anchor) is bounded above by the anchors' own reliability: a κ of 0.55 against single-annotator anchors with human–human κ of 0.60 means something entirely different from 0.55 against adjudicated consensus anchors with human–human κ of 0.90, and the protocol cannot distinguish "the judge is mediocre" from "the anchor set is noisy". The chapter already knows this — §6 requires exactly the missing discipline for non-generator instruments ("Dual-label every item independently, adjudicate disagreements ... and report chance-corrected inter-rater agreement") — but never applies it to the anchor set that gates every judge-driven decision. §8.4's assumption box acknowledges the adjacent risk ("a non-representative anchor set inflates a κ that won't transfer") without requiring the measurement that would detect it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to §5.7 step 1: the anchor set MUST be dual-labeled independently with disagreements adjudicated by a documented rule, and human–human chance-corrected agreement MUST be reported alongside κ(judge, anchor); the judge's κ is interpreted relative to that ceiling, and an anchor set whose own agreement is below the pre-registered judge bar cannot license any gate outcome. State which of the two label forms (individual or adjudicated) κ is computed against, since it changes the number.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.7 steps 2 and 7 (lines 283–296), §8.3 (lines 508–523), §6 parameter (lines 446–448)
findings.description: The protocol's central statistical requirement is a dangling reference, and its one piece of estimator guidance is wrong. §5.7 step 7 mandates "Report κ with a confidence interval, every time"; §8.3 defers the CI to chapter 04 ("Report κ with a confidence interval (chapter 04)"); §6 sizes the anchor set by "the κ confidence interval the decision needs (chapter 04)". Chapter 04 and references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS.md contain no κ content whatsoever — a case-insensitive search for kappa / κ / Cohen / Fleiss / inter-rater across both returns only one unrelated hit (Fleiss's m₀ correction for unbalanced clusters in the ICC section). Chapter 04's only sizing machinery is a McNemar-based paired-binary MDE expressed in discordance rate and N_eff, which does not size a κ CI. So the protocol's mandatory statistic cannot be computed by following the playbook, and §6's sample-size parameter is unactionable. Separately, §5.7 step 2's parenthetical "Report κ (Cohen's for two raters, weighted/Fleiss' for more)" mislabels weighted κ: weighted κ is for *two* raters on *ordinal* categories, not for more raters. A reader with two raters and an ordinal rubric — the modal judge-calibration case — is pointed away from the correct estimator.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a κ block to references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS.md and to chapter 04 §8: Cohen's κ and its asymptotic (or bootstrap) standard error, the CI construction, and a sample-size table or formula for a target CI half-width at plausible κ and marginal distributions — then have 03 §8.3 and §6 link to it. Fix step 2 to: "Cohen's κ for two raters with nominal categories; weighted κ (linear or quadratic, stated) for two raters with ordinal categories; Fleiss' κ for three or more raters."

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §6 "Instrument-validation investment by stakes tier", Tier-1 row (line 426), against §7 judge-trust gate (line 460) and 00 §9
findings.description: The rigor dial creates a Tier-1 judge exemption that the chapter's own gate and the global REJECTED list deny. The tier table says for Tier 1: "Judge calibration: None — avoid judges on adoption decisions." §7's gate is unconditional: "no judge score drives a decision until all seven steps of §5.7 are complete and reported." Chapter 00 §9's REJECTED entry is likewise unconditional: "trusting an uncalibrated judge's score for any decision." A Tier-1 reader gets two opposite instructions, and the natural reading of the tier table — uncalibrated judges are fine for direction-setting — is itself a decision (what to work on next), which the other two texts forbid. Since 00 §6's rule of proportion already escalates any Tier-3 decision made inside a Tier-1 project, the exemption is not needed in its current absolute form and the ambiguity is pure downside.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the Tier-1 cell state a scope rather than an absence: "None required, and no judge score may enter a comparison, an adoption or elimination decision, or any reported number; uncalibrated judge output is admissible only as unrecorded triage for choosing what to look at next." Then narrow §7's gate and 00 §9's REJECTED entry with the same carve-out wording so all three texts agree.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §6 "Contradiction: volume vs. curation (G20)", Decision rule, lines 415–420
findings.description: The contradiction is honestly surfaced but half-resolved by a pseudo-formula. "Weight by (grading-signal quality) × (marginal item cost) × (stakes tier)" is typeset as a computation while none of the three factors has a definition, a unit, or a scale, no threshold exists to compare the product against, and — decisively — the first two factors push in opposite directions: higher grading-signal quality argues for volume, higher marginal item cost argues for curation, so their product is not even directionally interpretable, and multiplying an ordinal stakes tier into it compounds the problem. The genuinely usable content is the prose that follows (cheap + deterministically gradable → volume; expensive-to-verify or judge-mediated → curation; Tier 3 curates regardless), which needs no formula. As written the formula is worse than nothing: it lends arithmetic authority to a judgment and invites a reader to compute a number that means nothing. Contrast §8, where every formula carries defined terms, a worked example, and an assumptions box.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the product and promote the prose to the decision rule, expressed as an explicit two-factor grid the reader can place themselves on — axis 1: is the item deterministically gradable at low marginal cost (yes → volume) or judge-mediated / expensive to verify (no → curation); axis 2: stakes tier, with Tier 3 forcing curation regardless. Add the one quantitative hook that is real: whichever direction is chosen, the smallest stratum must still resolve its required MDE (§6's corpus-size parameter), which is the binding constraint on shrinking a corpus.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.5 "Vendor decision-page lag", lines 290–301; §10 table row NV-MODELOPTQUANT-001 (line 430)
findings.description: The decision rule is sound but its supporting quantification is fabricated and self-contradictory within one paragraph. The setup says the decision page "does not mention the newer low-precision format the vendor's flagship release demonstrates and recommends **a month later**"; the decision rule three sentences on says such a page "can lag its own demonstrated flagship practice by **roughly a year**". Neither figure is derivable: sources.yaml gives NV-MODELOPTQUANT-001 `pub_date: null` and NV-MODELOPTQAD-001 `pub_date: null`; only NV-QADNEMOTRON-001 is dated (2026-08-17). The ledger's own note on the Unsloth row makes the general point explicitly — "staleness undatable from the page" — and this chapter's rule then correctly says to prefer a dated demonstration "over an undated or stale decision page", conceding the page is undated while the same paragraph calls it "a vendor's *dated* 'how to choose' page" and quantifies its lag. §10's advice to "check the as-of date before following" points at a date that does not exist.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop both numbers. State what the ledger supports: "the decision page is undated; the flagship demonstration is dated 2026-08-17 and the decision page still omits its format as of the 2026-08-21 verification." Rewrite the rule without a lag magnitude: "Prefer the most recently dated first-party demonstration over an undated or older decision page; where the page is undated, treat it as unverifiable for currency and record the as-of date of whichever source you follow." Replace §10's "check the as-of date" with "this page carries no publication date — treat as undatable."

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.2 taxonomy rows RC-10, RC-11, RC-12 (lines 185–187), against 07 §2 (lines 35–37) and 07 §5.1 rung 8/9 rows (lines 135–136)
findings.description: The bottom three classes cannot be assigned by the procedure the playbook requires. 07 §2 demands the reader arrive with a class already in hand ("A root-cause class ... not a symptom description. If you have only a symptom, return to chapter 03"), but the only stated discriminator between RC-10 ("lacks task-specific skill that demonstrably exists in obtainable training data") and RC-11 ("cannot do it at any budget") is 07's rung-8 evidence bar: "fine-tuning demonstrably insufficient, not merely untried" — i.e. you must already have run rung 7 to tell them apart. 09 §7 confirms the circularity by routing a failed ablation back to 07 to re-decide RC-10 vs RC-11 after the fact. RC-12 is worse: its evidence bar is "a staged, one-variable-at-a-time run of the whole ladder", so it is by construction a residual left after every other class is excluded. The taxonomy therefore presents three cost-ordered residual buckets as if they were ex-ante diagnoses, which undercuts the exactly-one-class claim and makes the rung-7/8/9 entry decisions look better grounded than they are.
findings.suggested_fix: Label RC-10/11/12 explicitly as provisional-residual classes in the table ("assigned provisionally after RC-1..RC-9 are excluded; distinguished only by the outcome of the rung they select"), and state the ordering rule that actually operates: attempt RC-10 first because it is the cheaper hypothesis, and treat a rung-7 INCONCLUSIVE or null as the evidence that reclassifies to RC-11 — which is what 09 §7 already prescribes. That keeps the taxonomy honest without weakening the ladder.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.2 canonical failure taxonomy (lines 174–192); GLOSSARY.md "pass-at-k vs pass-to-the-k" (line 454); 00 §6 Tier-3 row
findings.description: The taxonomy is not collectively exhaustive in a way the playbook elsewhere treats as first-order: there is no class for a system that has the capability but not the repeatability — high pass@1, collapsing pass^k on identical tasks at the same configuration. RC-2 is an infrastructure *defect*, RC-8 is budget exhaustion, RC-6 is an unstated task; none covers sampling stochasticity, and the ladder has no rung for the interventions that address it (decoding/sampling policy, self-consistency, retry/latching policy, reliability-targeted verification). The playbook takes this failure mode seriously everywhere else: the GLOSSARY defines pass^k precisely for it ("Stochastic systems can score high pass@1 and collapse at pass^k on identical tasks"), 00 §6 makes pass^k reliability claims a mandatory Tier-3 artifact, and EXT-AGENT-001 records the empirical basis ("gpt-4o agent pass^1>60% collapses <25% at pass^8"). A reader who measures exactly that has no RC class to record and no rung to work at. Note also that the GLOSSARY's execution-system definition omits decoding/sampling parameters from the frozen identity, so the same gap appears in the measurement-validity canon.
findings.suggested_fix: Either add a class (e.g. RC-8b or a renumbered "reliability/stochasticity gap — the capability is present but not repeatable at the required pass^k") mapped to rung 5 or a new rung 5b covering decoding policy, self-consistency and retry/latching; or, if the intent is that this is out of the taxonomy's scope, say so explicitly under the table and point to chapters 04 and 08. Also add decoding/sampling parameters to the execution-system field list in the GLOSSARY.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.1 rung 1 row and rung 3 row (lines 128, 130); GLOSSARY.md "tool contract" (lines 618–623)
findings.description: Byte-level transport fidelity is assigned to two different rungs and two different RC classes in the same table. Rung 1 (RC-2, infrastructure/runtime) lists as its cheap diagnostic "byte-equivalence check through every proxy [CASE: CASE-008]"; rung 3 (RC-4, tool/API contract) lists as its evidence "schema/grammar enforcement verified against the actual transport bytes" and as its cheap diagnostic "a small transport byte-equivalence smoke test". The GLOSSARY settles it the third way, folding "byte-level transport fidelity" inside the definition of tool contract (RC-4/rung 3), while CASE-008 is titled a transport-serialization defect and is cited at rung 1. So the single case the playbook uses most to teach this failure has no stable class, and a reader diagnosing a serialization defect gets rung 1 or rung 3 depending on which cell they read.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick one home and cross-reference the other: put transport-byte fidelity under RC-2/rung 1 when the corruption is introduced by the serving stack, proxy, or transport independent of any tool (CASE-008's shape), and restrict rung 3's byte check to schema/grammar conformance of tool payloads. Then narrow the GLOSSARY's tool-contract definition accordingly, or state there that transport fidelity is shared between RC-2 and RC-4 with the stated discriminator.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §2 "The intervention ladder card", rungs 8 and 9 (lines 44–45), against 07 §5.1 (lines 135–136)
findings.description: The card presents itself as the same content as its sources ("§2. The intervention ladder card (00 §4 P3; 03 §5.2; 07)") but states materially weaker escalation bars for the two most expensive rungs. For rung 8 the card requires "evidence cheaper rungs cannot close the gap", which a reader can satisfy by argument without ever having attempted fine-tuning; 07 §5.1 requires "A pre-registered transfer/ceiling test shows the residual failure is not predictable from anything short of the model's own weights — fine-tuning demonstrably insufficient, not merely untried". For rung 9 the card requires only "a documented method decision record"; 07 requires "A staged, one-variable-at-a-time run of the whole ladder ... shows the residual gap tracks the *topology*, not any single component". Since 14 is the checklist chapter — the artifact a reader actually consults at decision time — the weaker text is the one that will bind in practice, and it licenses exactly the expensive premature escalation the ladder exists to prevent.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the two cells with compressed but faithful restatements of 07's bars ("rung 8: pre-registered transfer/ceiling test; fine-tuning demonstrably insufficient, not merely untried"; "rung 9: staged one-variable-at-a-time ladder run showing the gap tracks topology, plus an MDR"), and add a line under the card stating that where the card and 07 §5.1 differ, 07 governs — the same precedence rule the GLOSSARY already asserts for itself.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.5 (lines 249–301); chapter 07 contains no doctrine marker anywhere
findings.description: 07 §5.5 prescribes a full acceptance procedure — a MUST/MUST NOT on gating quantization by the project's own eval, a recovery-percentage bar, a four-step escalation ladder, a portability principle, and a STOP CONDITION — with no internal execution record and no doctrine-not-yet-exercised marker. A search of all chapters shows 07 is the only methodology chapter with zero markers, while 02, 05, 06, 08, 09, 10, 12 and 13 all carry them. The chapter's own §10 concedes the external sources do not supply the procedure: NV-NVFP4PLAYBOOK-001 "No acceptance-gate procedure — 'we recommend running evaluations' with no threshold", NV-MODELOPTQAD-001 "No acceptance threshold of its own", and NV-QADNEMOTRON-001 is "one vendor's internal practice on its own benchmark suite, not doctrine for yours" (sources.yaml records it as evidence_strength: case-study, freshness: snapshot). No INT-CASE in 07's §13 relates to quantization, and §8's recovery worked example is flagged "illustrative, invented numbers". Under 00 P12 and the chapter's own standard this procedure needs the marker; 09 marks a structurally identical unexercised procedure ("Rig before model") correctly.
findings.suggested_fix: Add at the head of §5.5: "*status: doctrine — not yet exercised (see §7 for what validation would look like)* — this playbook has no internal record of a quantization acceptance gate; the recovery-bar shape is adapted from one vendor's demonstrated practice on its own benchmark suite, and the escalation ladder is inference from the vendor's stated recovery step." Same treatment for 03 §5.8's contamination re-test and canary-string procedures, which sources.yaml records as a "new action" (EXT-EVAL-007) rather than an exercised one.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §6 parameter table, QLoRA VRAM row (line 174); §10 vendor table rows for EXT-FT-003 and EXT-UNSLOTH-001 (lines 287–288)
findings.description: Two problems in a row a reader will use to size hardware. (a) Attribution looks inverted: the floors are credited to EXT-FT-003 "(cross-checked [EXT-UNSLOTH-001])", and §10 lists EXT-FT-003 as [FOLLOW] supplying "Verified VRAM floors by base-model size". But sources.yaml dates EXT-FT-003 to the QLoRA paper (arXiv:2305.14314, 2023), whose model sizes are the 2023 LLaMA family, while the quoted sizes (9B, 27B) belong to model families released after it; the EXT-UNSLOTH-001 row is the one whose note records these figures as an exact live match ("9B 6.5GB QLoRA/24GB LoRA; 27B 22GB/64GB; 70B 41GB/164GB — stated as absolute minimums"). The primary and the cross-check appear to be the wrong way round, which matters because the two sources have very different freshness properties (the Unsloth row notes "Unsloth publishes no dates — staleness undatable"). (b) The derived rule is wrong in the unsafe direction: "16-bit LoRA roughly 3× higher" understates the source's own ratios, which run 2.9× (27B: 22→64) to 4.0× (70B: 41→164), with 9B at 3.7× (6.5→24). A reader applying "roughly 3×" to the 9B floor computes 19.5 GB and concludes a 20 GB card suffices, where the cited source states 24 GB as an absolute minimum — and the row itself warns "these are floors, not comfortable operating points".
findings.suggested_fix: Cite EXT-UNSLOTH-001 as the primary for the by-size floors with EXT-FT-003 as the method reference, or confirm the QLoRA paper actually carries these sizes before leaving it primary. Replace the multiplier with the source's actual paired figures (9B 6.5/24 GB, 27B 22/64 GB, 70B 41/164 GB QLoRA/16-bit LoRA) and, if a rule of thumb is wanted, state it as "3–4×, and never round down when sizing to a floor".

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §8 rescue-fraction worked example, lines 371–377
findings.description: The flagship gate's worked example teaches three things the playbook forbids elsewhere. (a) It reads a point estimate against a band with no interval: "the treatment arm passes the deterministic scorer on 9: f_rescue = 9/20 = 45% ... If the pre-registered GO band is f_rescue ≥ 30%, ... the verdict is **GO**." A 95% Wilson interval on 9/20 is roughly [0.26, 0.66] — its lower bound sits below the 30% band, and at the example's own sufficiency floor of n_min = 12 the interval is wider still. So the illustrated design cannot resolve the illustrated band, which is 00 §9's REJECTED "Promoting sub-MDE margins to decisions" and P9's INCONCLUSIVE requirement. (b) It inserts an unpre-registered escape clause into a pre-registered band — "absent contradictory evidence in the classification of the remaining 11, the verdict is GO" — where §5.2 step 5 requires any deviation to be a *written* override, and 00 §9's first REJECTED item is the unpriced escape hatch. (c) It reports a rescue rate with no selection-effect caveat, although §5.3 step 6 requires one "wherever a rescue/conversion rate is reported" and f_rescue is conditioned on the reconfirmed subset (20 of 25) while the GO decision licenses an experiment on the full population.
findings.suggested_fix: Rework the example to carry an interval and an explicit sufficiency check against it, and set n_min from the width needed to separate the band rather than from a bare count — or, if the gate is deliberately a screening device rather than an inferential one, say so at §5.2 step 3 and require the verdict to be printed as RANKED/screening under chapter 04's screening-vs-inference rule, with the interval still reported. Delete "absent contradictory evidence..." or replace it with "a decision owner may override the band only via a written override recorded in the diagnostic run's ledger entry (§5.2 step 5)". Add the §5.3 step 6 selection-effect sentence to the example.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.7 step 2 (lines 283–288) and §8.3 worked example (lines 518–523)
findings.description: A source the ledger classifies as do-not-depend is the sole empirical warrant for a mandatory reporting rule, cited with no strength marker at the point of use. sources.yaml records EXT-JUDGE-003 (arXiv:2606.19544) as classification: REFERENCE, evidence_strength: contested, maturity: new, pub_date 2026 — and the GLOSSARY defines REFERENCE as "consult, don't depend". The chapter depends on it twice: step 2 justifies the κ-not-raw-agreement MUST with "one large multi-judge study measured a 33–41 percentage-point deflation between the two [EXT-JUDGE-003]", and §8.3 anchors its worked example to "the kind of deflation measured across a large multi-judge study". Neither mention carries a contested/REFERENCE marker, so a reader sees a single-year-old unreplicated result rendered as settled — the exact pattern P12 names ("A recent paper is never rendered as law"). The irony is that the rule does not need the paper: that raw agreement overstates chance-corrected agreement is a property of the κ definition, provable from §8.3's own formula.
findings.suggested_fix: Ground the MUST in the arithmetic — "κ subtracts the agreement expected from the raters' marginals; whenever labels are unbalanced, raw agreement will exceed κ by construction" — and demote EXT-JUDGE-003 to a corroborating illustration carrying its ledger status inline: "a single recent multi-judge study (contested, REFERENCE) reports deflations of 33–41 points". Apply the same at §8.3.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.7 doctrine marker, lines 275–276
findings.description: The marker's parenthetical appears to be copy-pasted from §6's and does not make sense in place: "*status: doctrine — not yet exercised (see §5.5 for the generator-derived instrument this protocol stands in for)*". §5.5 is the instrument-validation checklist (reachability, inversions, gold-answer gate, determinism, frontier saturation); it is not an analog of, and does not stand in for, judge calibration. §6's identical parenthetical ("see §5.5 for the generator-derived analog these protocols stand in for", line 389) is coherent because §6 is about replacing generator-derived ground truth. The doctrine marker's own convention elsewhere in the playbook is "see X for what validation would look like" (10, 12, 13), which is more useful.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace with "*status: doctrine — not yet exercised (see §7's judge-trust gate for what validation would look like: a scored anchor set, κ with CI against a pre-registered bar, and a completed bias-audit report)*".

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.2 step 3 pseudocode comment, lines 168–172, against §7 decision tree (line 327) and §9 (lines 403–405)
findings.description: The pseudocode's explanatory comment forbids only one of the two verdicts the rest of the chapter forbids. It reads "(An underpowered diagnostic tells you the premise is unmeasured, not that it is false — it can never license DROP.)", while §7's tree says "yes → INCONCLUSIVE / RE-SCOPE (never DROP; never GO)" and §9 names "Underpowered diagnostic read as GO" as a REJECTED pattern. The pseudocode is the piece a reader will transcribe into their pre-registration, so the weaker comment is the one likely to propagate.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the comment: "— it can never license DROP, and a favorable point estimate below n_min can never license GO either (§9)."

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §5.3 corpus design bullets (lines 196–217) and §5.8 leakage bullets (lines 306–321)
findings.description: These bullets carry normative force — including a bare "MUST" in §5.3 ("Filler/background content MUST be produced by the same generation path as primary content") and in effect in §5.8 — but no A-to-H badge and no evidence-strength label, while the same chapter's §4 and §5.1 label every principle and default. 00 P12 and the GLOSSARY's evidence-strength-labels entry state that the annotation is carried by "every principle and default". The §5.3 pipeline-bypass rule is additionally hedged in its own justification ("tends to carry an artifact") yet stated as a MUST, so a reader cannot tell whether it is a first-principles invariant or a heuristic from one project.
findings.suggested_fix: Badge and label the normative bullets in §5.3 and §5.8 — most are [DEFAULT] (heuristic) or [DEFAULT] (inference — first-principles), with the pipeline-bypass rule plausibly [DEFAULT] (case-study) if CASE-004 or the source project's corpus work supports it.

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: §10 vendor table, NV-TOOLCALLTUTORIAL-001 row (line 574), against 09 §6 tool-calling row (line 176)
findings.description: Two chapters disagree about what transfers from the same source. 03 §10 calls it "a concrete §6 volume resolution" — i.e. evidence settling the volume-vs-curation contradiction — citing "~85/15 synthesis/independent split, scaled past 500 samples to ~93% on a held-out golden set". 09 §6's row for the same source says the opposite about transferability: "your own tool surface; **the ratio, not the absolute count, is the transferable part**". If the absolute count does not transfer, one tutorial reaching 93% on one tool surface is not a resolution of a general corpus-sizing contradiction.
findings.suggested_fix: Align 03 §10 with 09 §6: describe it as "one worked instance of the volume position on a deterministically gradable task family; the split ratio and the independent-golden-set pattern transfer, the sample count does not".

findings.reviewer: Adversarial scientific review — methodology chapters (03, 07, 09) of Adaptive AI Systems Playbook v0.1.0
findings.location: "silent failure" entry, lines 561–565
findings.description: The entry says verification gaps "(RC-7) rank high in diagnosis", which reads as a claim about the taxonomy's priority ordering. The only ordering the taxonomy actually asserts is that RC-1 ranks first (03 §5.2, line 189); RC-7 maps to rung 4, mid-ladder, and is reached only after rungs 0–3 clear. The phrasing invites a reader to jump to RC-7 ahead of cheaper classes, and it is the second place (with the RC-1/RC-7 wording overlap) where RC-7's scope is left loose.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite as: "...and the reason the in-system verification gap (RC-7, rung 4) is checked explicitly rather than assumed absent — a verifier that passes failures silently produces no signal of its own."

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §5 Step 9 (line 207) and §7 Freeze gate (lines 265–277), vs. templates/EXPERIMENT_CONTRACT.md §8/§10/Freeze Checklist (lines 179, 211–221, 352) and 14 §6.1 (line 257)
findings.description: The freeze point is stated three incompatible ways, and the strict version makes the mandatory first deliverable unproducible for a greenfield project. 04 §5 Step 9 says "Commit the contract (content-hash bound) before the first iterate-split call"; 04 §7's Freeze gate says "Before the first iterate-split item executes" the statistical plan — "clustering unit, ICC, DEFF, N_eff, MDE" — MUST be written; 14 §6.1 repeats it ("Committed before the first iterate-split call" + "Clustering unit, ICC, DEFF, N_eff, MDE ... written before data"). But the contract template sources exactly those values from the iterate split: §8 "Pilot MDE: [the MDE computed on the pilot/iterate-split data]", §10 "Expected discordance: [...from pilot data]", §10 "ICC estimate and source". The template's own gate is looser — "before any iterate-split evidence is used for inference" (line 352) — and the flagship WALKTHROUGH follows the looser reading ("ICC = 0.15 (iterate-estimated)"; "Freeze checklist: all eight items checked before qualification-split execution began"). 04 §2 offers only "ideally, a prior ICC estimate from a related suite," which a no-eval/no-incumbent project does not have, while 04 §8 and STATISTICS_FORMULAS §2 forbid the obvious workaround ("never assumed zero"; "Never assume it — estimate it"). The adopter is therefore trapped between an unsatisfiable gate and a forbidden shortcut, and the path of least resistance — borrowing the walkthrough's 0.15 or the template example's 0.09 — is precisely 04 §6's prohibition on copying another project's numbers. An ICC borrowed too low inflates N_eff, shrinks the stated MDE, and licenses CONFIRMED verdicts the design cannot support: the exact failure mode CASE-002 exists to document. 14 §8's release consistency check names this class of drift as a release blocker, so this one slipped its own net.
findings.suggested_fix: Name the two-stage freeze explicitly in 04 and make the three statements agree. Concretely: (a) restate 04 §5 Step 9 and §7 as "frozen before the first qualification-split item executes, and before any iterate-split evidence is used for inference"; (b) add an explicit cold-start path — freeze with a declared prior/provisional ICC labelled as such, run an ICC-estimation pilot on the iterate split (or under the non-promotable diagnostic run kind of 04 §4), then revise DEFF/N_eff/MDE via the §7 amendment procedure, whose five conditions this satisfies by construction (pre-registered procedure, iterate-split-only evidence, committed before qualify/confirm); (c) add an EXPERIMENT_CONTRACT §10 field for "ICC source: prior / pilot-estimated" with the revision rule, mirroring 01 §5.5's cold-start discipline; (d) fix 14 §6.1's checklist line to match.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §3 Artifacts, lines 85–95
findings.description: §3 requires "Every model artifact by content hash + upstream identity" with a mandatory "Content hash / digest" column, and states flatly that "An artifact identified only by a human-readable name (e.g. a model family and a release date) is not pinned." For a BAA'd managed-API deployment — the execution surface archetype A is built on, and the only one admissible for my project — a content hash of hosted weights is unobtainable in principle. The template gives no managed-API row, no fallback, and no N/A guidance for this specific case; the WALKTHROUGH, which is archetype A and API-only, silently omits §3 from its condensed contract rather than showing what to write. The mitigation does exist elsewhere and is good — 02 §5 Step 1 hedges correctly ("for every execution-system component that has one"), 02 §6 says a managed-API-only project needs the provider-redeploy probe, 02 §5 Step 2 defines it, and the WALKTHROUGH's frozen identity uses a "provider model-version string" — but none of that is cross-referenced from §3. A team following the template literally either fabricates a digest, deletes the section (which "Delete No Section" forbids), or concludes that managed-API comparisons cannot be pinned and quietly abandons the discipline.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a managed-API row and a sentence to §3: where no content hash is obtainable, pin by (provider model-version string + endpoint/region + as-of timestamp + a recorded provider-redeploy probe result per 02 §5 Step 2), and state that the comparability claim is scoped to the probed window. Cross-reference 02 §6's "a managed-API-only project needs the provider-redeploy probe and nothing else from this list." Fill §3 in the WALKTHROUGH's condensed contract so the API-only case is shown, not skipped.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §5.1 four-layer table (lines 138–145), §5.3 corpus design (lines 195–217), §8.2
findings.description: The task-ontology derivation presents one output shape as universal: "The output is a four-layer closed vocabulary" — symptom category / root cause / sanctioned action / forbidden claim — with root cause "scored by exact match against the closed set" and sanctioned action "scored by membership in that cause's cause-to-action table," both gated as breaking changes. That model is specific to diagnose-and-act tasks (the running example is helpdesk triage, and §8.2's lookup-ceiling arithmetic only means anything for a symptom→cause mapping). For a generate-and-extract task — my visit summaries and follow-up flags, and equally summarization, drafting, or field extraction — there is no symptom layer and no sanctioned-action set; only 'forbidden claim' transfers cleanly. §5.3's mandatory-sounding corpus design inherits the same assumption ("Keep at least one action or label valid for no item" presumes an action set). The evidence that this doesn't generalize is inside the playbook: none of its own worked examples instantiates the four layers — the WALKTHROUGH uses seven task-type classes, SYNTH-03 a 12-field schema, SYNTH-01 an unstructured 'task ontology from 400 transcripts' — yet none acknowledges substituting a different shape. A new adopter on a generative task is left to invent the ontology model, which is the single largest piece of work in M2.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the four-layer vocabulary explicitly task-shape-conditional and add at least one alternate shape. Suggested: a table mapping task shape → ontology layers (diagnose-and-act → symptom/root-cause/action/forbidden-claim; extract-to-schema → field set/field-criticality strata/forbidden-value classes; generate/summarize → required-fact set/omission classes/forbidden-claim set/stratification dimensions), keeping 'forbidden claim' as the universal layer and marking 'sanctioned action' as applicable only where the system selects an action. Note in §5.3 which corpus-design bullets are action-set-dependent.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §6 "Non-generator instruments (G3)", lines 384–400, against §5.5/§8.1 and §5.3
findings.description: Every instrument-validation mechanism the chapter makes mandatory assumes a code-driven generator: reachability ceilings are computed by "replay[ing] the evidence plan against the built corpus" (§5.5, §8.1), the determinism check requires "regenerate the full corpus independently; compare a canonical content digest," and §5.3 requires per-instance generator consistency and "background content through the real pipeline." None of that is executable on a corpus of real patient-clinician transcripts with human-adjudicated gold — which is the normal condition for regulated projects and, per the routing tree's branch 1, for every project arriving without a trusted eval. The alternative path is §6's three bullets (dual-label + adjudicate + κ; sampled-audit ceiling proxy; judge-mediated behind §5.7), marked doctrine and exercised in no worked example. The playbook self-identifies this (PLAYBOOK_BUILD_PLAN.md G3: "the reachability/determinism apparatus assumes a code-driven generator") and dispositions it COVERED-AS-DOCTRINE, so this is a proportionality complaint, not a dishonesty one — but the ratio is roughly 60 lines of mandatory generator machinery to 3 bullets for the path most adopters are actually on, and §6 leaves the practical questions unanswered: how large the sampled audit must be for the ceiling proxy to be trustworthy, whether the auditing clinician may be one of the gold annotators, and how the gold-answer gate and cross-arm disagreement review are run without a generator.
findings.suggested_fix: Promote §6's non-generator protocols from three bullets to a numbered procedure parallel to §5.5, with: a sampled-audit sizing rule tied to the ceiling precision the stratum's threshold needs; an independence requirement between ceiling auditors and gold annotators; non-generator substitutes for the gold-answer gate (re-score adjudicated gold through the scorer) and the determinism check (annotation-batch/guideline-version digest, which EVAL_SUITE_RELEASE_CONTRACT.md line 66 already contemplates); and route one worked example (SYNTH-08 is the natural host) through the human-annotated path so it is exercised at least on paper.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §5 (ten obligations), §6 privacy-class table (lines 195–204), §13 G6 disposition — and the absence across all chapters
findings.description: Nothing in the playbook addresses regulated personal data in the evaluation corpus itself. A repository-wide search for HIPAA / PHI / de-identification / anonymization returns exactly one incidental hit ("anonymized claim sample" in an EVAL_SUITE_RELEASE_CONTRACT example). Chapter 13 covers the adjacent problems well — telemetry/trajectory privacy classes, redaction-before-persist, clean-room boundary, ground-truth isolation — and is honest that its G6 half is doctrine because "this playbook's own source project ran on structurally synthetic data." But archetype E is *defined* by regulatory dominance, and for any E adopter the first blocking question is corpus-level, not telemetry-level: may raw regulated content be copied into an eval store at all; must it be de-identified before annotation; who may see it (my clinical-informatics annotators must read PHI to label, which collides with §4's two-layer isolation framing); how long may a frozen suite retain it against §6's retention parameter; and — the measurement-validity consequence the playbook would normally be first to name — whether de-identifying the corpus shifts the input distribution enough to invalidate ceilings and transfer to production. 03 §5.8's leakage controls and 12 §5.6's "apply the privacy filter before harvesting" both stop short of the corpus-construction decision.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 13 §5 obligation (and a pointer from 03 §5.3/§5.4) covering regulated content in the eval corpus: an explicit decision — de-identify, tokenize, or hold raw under access control — with the trade-off stated in measurement-validity terms; an annotator-access rule that reconciles 'humans must read the data to label it' with two-layer isolation (isolate the *gold labels* from the model-facing path, not the source content from the annotator); a retention rule for frozen suites; and a required note in EVAL_SUITE_RELEASE_CONTRACT recording which transformation the corpus underwent and what was verified about its effect on the task. Flag it `doctrine — not yet exercised` like the rest of G6.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §8 MDE (lines 342–366) and references/STATISTICS_FORMULAS.md §3, against 03 §5.7 and 00 §6's Tier-3 row
findings.description: The playbook mandates judge calibration wherever judges are used at Tier 3 (00 §6; 03 §5.7) and mandates a pre-computed MDE for every comparison (04 §8), but never connects them. Every MDE and power form in 04 §8 and STATISTICS_FORMULAS §1–§5 assumes the per-item outcome is observed without error; the assumptions boxes list clustering, pairing, binary-ness and small-n, but not label noise. When the outcome is produced by a judge at κ≈0.7 or by dual human annotators with imperfect agreement, measurement error in the outcome attenuates the observed paired difference toward zero and inflates the N_eff required to detect a real effect — so a design sized from these formulas is systematically underpowered exactly on the judge-graded dimension the playbook flags as highest-risk. The practical consequence for my project is a false INCONCLUSIVE (or, if the noise is asymmetric between arms, a false CONFIRMED) on the narrative-quality half of the comparison. 03 §6's parameter "Judge calibration sample size — size the human-anchor set to resolve the κ confidence interval the decision needs (chapter 04)" points at 04 for machinery that 04 does not contain.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short section to STATISTICS_FORMULAS (and a line in 04 §8's assumptions) on outcome-measurement error: state that a noisy grader attenuates the observed effect and inflates required N, give the attenuation relationship you are willing to stand behind for a binary outcome at a measured agreement rate, and add a contract §10 field "grader reliability used in the power calculation (κ or agreement rate, and its source)." At minimum, add a 'when this breaks' bullet to §3a/§3b naming judge- and annotator-graded outcomes, so a team is warned even before a formula exists.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §6 volume-vs-curation decision rule (lines 402–420) and §6 corpus-size parameter (lines 438–442), against 04 §6 α/power parameter (lines 240–244)
findings.description: Three normative statements collide at Tier 3 with no precedence rule, and the collision is decisive for any project whose labels are expensive. 03 §6 resolves volume-vs-curation with "Tier 3 projects SHOULD curate regardless of grading cost" — fewer items. 03 §6's corpus-size parameter says "Size the smallest stratum to the MDE it needs to resolve (chapter 04), not a fixed item count." 04 §6 says "A Tier-3 decision SHOULD tighten one or both [α and power]" — which raises required N_eff, on top of a DEFF that clustering by clinician and visit type will make substantial. Curate-hard and tighten-power are directly opposed on N, and the MDE-driven sizing rule cannot arbitrate because it presupposes the ICC and discordance a cold-start project doesn't have yet (see the freeze finding). For me the collision is the whole plan: clinician-hours cap the corpus at a few hundred dual-labeled items, which at a realistic ICC leaves an MDE plausibly larger than the quality difference I need to resolve — and the playbook never tells me that discovering this *before* spending 150 clinician-hours is the point of the exercise.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an explicit precedence rule and a feasibility check. Suggested: (1) state that when curation and power targets conflict, the licensed moves are to widen the MDE and say so in the contract, reduce the number of arms, or narrow the population — never to silently keep the tightened α/power on a corpus that cannot support it; (2) add a pre-M2 'label-budget feasibility probe' — given achievable annotator throughput, a plausible ICC range, and the effect the decision needs, compute whether any affordable corpus resolves it, and treat a negative answer as a 01 §5.3 kill-criteria event before the labeling spend, not after.

findings.reviewer: Practitioner-portability review — senior engineer, telehealth visit-summarization + follow-up flagging (HIPAA, BAA'd managed APIs, ~8k calls/wk, 2 ML engineers + clinical-informatics reviewers, no eval, no incumbent)
findings.location: §5 Table 10.1 shadow/canary rows (lines 125–131) and rollback rehearsal step 1 (lines 145–151)
findings.description: The promotion pipeline assumes an automated incumbent exists. The shadow row reads "only the incumbent's response reaches the user" with the exit gate "outcome-distribution comparison ... shows no regression beyond the pre-registered tolerance." For a greenfield deployment — archetype A by definition, and my E project, both reached via routing-tree branch 2 answering 'no incumbent' — there is no incumbent arm; the baseline is a human process producing an artifact of a different kind, so 'no regression' is undefined and 10 gives no substitute. SYNTH-08 quietly solves it with "94% agreement with human triage, 0.6% regret cases" and its promotion gate turns on "measured shadow agreement above a pre-registered floor, regret rate below a pre-registered ceiling" — but 'regret' is used as a gate metric in 08 §5, 14 §4, SYNTH-04 and SYNTH-08 and defined nowhere, including the GLOSSARY, and the human-as-baseline design (who adjudicates disagreements, whether the clinician's own note is gold or merely a comparator, how clinician-authorship clustering enters the statistics) is never specified. Separately, §5's rollback state list enumerates in-flight generation, KV/session state, adapter references and cached tool results — all inference-side. It has no category for effects already committed to an external system of record, which for me is the only thing that actually matters: rolling back the model does not unwrite summaries already pushed to the EHR.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a greenfield/human-baseline variant to Table 10.1: define the shadow comparison against the current human process (agreement rate, regret rate, and the adjudication procedure for disagreements), define 'regret' in the GLOSSARY, and note that clinician/operator identity is a clustering unit for the shadow statistics. Add a sixth item to the rollback-rehearsal state list: side effects already written to external systems of record — what the rollback must retract, amend, or flag, and who is notified — since a write-capable Tier-3 deployment is exactly the case 13's tool-permission gate anticipates.
